Archaeocyathus.note: A cup-shaped reef builder of the early Cambrian, sponge-grade animals that made the first animal reefs and were gone by the middle of the period.

Archimedes.note: A bryozoan built as a corkscrew: a lacy fan wound round a spiral axis, named for the screw, and a rock-former in Mississippian limestones.

Astraspis.note: One of the oldest vertebrates with a skeleton, a jawless fish clad in mosaic bony plates, from the Ordovician of Colorado.

Atrypa.note: A round, finely ribbed brachiopod with a spiral feeding organ inside, in nearly every Silurian and Devonian shelf sea in the world.

Aviculopecten.note: A scallop-like bivalve of the late Palaeozoic, in every shelf sea from the Mississippian to the end of the Permian.

Bananogmius.note: A deep-bodied plethodid fish of the Niobrara sea with a fan-like dorsal fin the length of its back.

Belemnitella.note: A Late Cretaceous belemnite whose bullet-shaped guards fill the Maastricht chalk; its oxygen isotopes were among the first used to read past sea temperatures.

Bellerophon.note: A planispiral snail-like mollusc, coiled in one plane like a tiny nautilus, grazing Carboniferous and Permian sea floors.

Calymene.note: The 'Dudley bug', a trilobite so abundant in the Silurian limestone of the English Midlands that the town put it on its coat of arms.

Cheirolepis.note: One of the earliest ray-finned fishes, a fast predator of the Devonian lakes of Scotland and Quebec, ancestral in form to half the vertebrates alive.

Cladoselache.note: An early shark from the Cleveland Shale, preserved with skin and muscle: a fast open-water hunter with the terminal mouth of a fish rather than a shark's underslung one.

Clidastes.note: A slender, fast mosasaur of shallow water, the smallest of the Kansas chalk mosasaurs at two to four metres.

Climacograptus.note: A single-stemmed graptolite with square-cut cups, the drifting plankton of Late Ordovician black shales on every continent.

Coccosteus.note: A half-metre arthrodire of the Old Red Sandstone lakes and seas of Scotland, armoured over the head and trunk and naked behind.

Composita.note: A smooth, rounded brachiopod, the single most abundant shell of Carboniferous and Permian limestones in North America.

Constellaria.note: A branching bryozoan whose colonies are dotted with star-shaped mounds; in the Cincinnatian it is a rock-forming fossil.

Cretoxyrhina.note: The 'Ginsu shark', seven metres long, whose bite marks are on the bones of mosasaurs and plesiosaurs from Kansas to Europe.

Cryptoclidus.note: A long-necked plesiosaur of the Oxford Clay with a hundred needle teeth, netting small fish and squid.

Cryptolithus.note: The lace-collar trilobite: blind, with a pitted fringe around the head that filtered the mud it ploughed through.

Cymbospondylus.note: An early ichthyosaur up to seventeen metres long with an eel-like body and no dorsal fin, from Nevada's Middle Triassic sea.

Dactylioceras.note: The Whitby ammonite, ribbed and evolute, once carved with snakes' heads and sold as the serpents St Hilda turned to stone.

Dalmanites.note: A trilobite with a long tail spine and large crescent eyes, a swimmer or fast crawler of the Silurian shelf.

Didymograptus.note: The tuning-fork graptolite, two branches hanging from a float; a colonial drifter whose fossils zone the Early Ordovician worldwide.

Durania.note: A barrel-shaped rudist, one of the strange bivalves that grew in thickets and built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous tropics in place of corals.

Edestus.note: The 'scissor-tooth shark', with a single blade of teeth in each jaw that never shed; a Pennsylvanian predator the size of a great white.

Elasmosaurus.note: A plesiosaur with seventy-two neck vertebrae and a neck seven metres long, from the Kansas chalk; its first describer put the head on the tail.
Elasmosaurus.conf_note: Asian 'Elasmosaurus' records are old referrals; the genus is Kansas

Eldredgeops.note: The Devonian trilobite of New York and Ohio, once called Phacops rana, whose eye lenses were read for the evolution of vision.

Elrathia.note: The trilobite everyone has held: Elrathia kingii from Utah's Wheeler Shale, quarried by the million from a low-oxygen shelf it had almost to itself.

Exogyra.note: A thick, coiled oyster with a spiral beak, cemented to the Cretaceous sea floor in beds you can walk on in Texas and Alabama.

Flexicalymene.note: The enrolled trilobite of the Cincinnati hills, found curled into a ball by the thousand; the commonest trilobite of Late Ordovician North America.

Girtyocoelia.note: A sphinctozoan sponge, a string of beads with a canal through them, one of the builders of the Permian Reef of Texas.

Globotruncana.note: A planktonic foraminifer with a double keel, the zone fossil of the Late Cretaceous ocean; the K-Pg boundary clay is full of its broken shells.

Goniatites.note: The goniatite that names its group: a globular ammonoid with zigzag sutures, a swimmer of Mississippian seas on every continent.

Heliolites.note: A 'sun coral', a tabulate whose tubes stand in a honeycomb of finer ones, building Silurian and Devonian reefs with Favosites and Halysites.

Hexagonaria.note: The Petoskey stone: a colonial rugose coral of Devonian reefs whose six-sided corallites turn up as pebbles on Lake Michigan beaches.

Hoploscaphites.note: A hook-shaped scaphitid ammonite of the Pierre Shale and the Maastrichtian chalk, one of the very last ammonites before the impact.

Hybodus.note: A hybodont shark with a spine before each dorsal fin and two kinds of teeth, for fish and for shellfish; the commonest shark of Mesozoic seas and rivers.

Ichthyornis.note: A tern-sized seabird with teeth, skimming the Western Interior Seaway; among the closest known relatives of modern birds.

Isorophus.note: An edrioasteroid, a disc of an echinoderm that cemented itself to shells and fed with five curved arms; a group with no living relatives.

Kockelella.note: A Silurian conodont, known from tooth-like elements a millimetre long that zone the Wenlock and Ludlow worldwide.

Leedsichthys.note: The largest ray-finned fish that has ever lived, sixteen metres of filter-feeder from the Oxford Clay, straining the Jurassic sea like a whale shark.

Leptaena.note: A wrinkled, flat-lying brachiopod with a sharp bend at the edge, one of the longest-lived shell genera of the Palaeozoic.

Leptodus.note: A brachiopod so modified for reef life it looks like an oyster: cemented, with a comb of internal ridges; one of the odd forms of the Permian reefs of Texas and the Tethys.

Lithiotis.note: A tall, wafer-thin bivalve that grew in dense upright thickets, the reef-builder of the Early Jurassic Tethys when corals were scarce.

Lophophyllidium.note: A small solitary horn coral of Pennsylvanian and Permian shelves, standing alone in the mud between the brachiopod beds.

Manticoceras.note: A Late Devonian goniatite whose disappearance marks the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, one of the five great ones.

Marrella.note: The commonest animal of the Burgess Shale, a thumbnail-sized arthropod with sweeping head spines; thousands of specimens, no close living relative.

Metriorhynchus.note: A crocodile rebuilt for the open sea: flippers, a tail fin, no armour, hunting fish and ammonites in the Oxford Clay.

Micraster.note: The heart urchin of the English chalk, whose changing shape up through the cliffs was one of the first fossil lineages read as evolution.

Mixosaurus.note: A metre-long early ichthyosaur with a fish's tail only half formed, from the Middle Triassic of the Alps, China and Nevada.

Monotis.note: A thin-shelled bivalve that drifted or lay in shoals over the whole Late Triassic ocean; its beds date Norian rocks from Alaska to New Zealand.

Neospirifer.note: A winged, strongly ribbed spiriferid brachiopod, common enough in the Permian to have been used as a guide fossil across Pangaea's shelves.

Nyctosaurus.note: A small pterosaur of the Kansas chalk with an antler-like crest half again as long as its skull.

Olenus.note: The late Cambrian trilobite of the Baltic alum shales, living in black oxygen-poor mud that preserved it in its thousands.

Opabinia.note: Five eyes and a hose-like proboscis ending in a claw; the Burgess Shale animal that drew laughter when first described.

Ophthalmosaurus.note: An ichthyosaur with eyes the size of dinner plates, the largest of any vertebrate relative to its body, for hunting squid in the dark.

Orthoceras.note: The straight-shelled nautiloid of the Baltic 'Orthoceras limestone', a metre-long swimmer whose chambered shells pave the floors of Swedish churches.

Ottoia.note: A burrowing priapulid worm, the commonest predator of the Burgess Shale sea floor, found with hyoliths in its gut.

Pachydiscus.note: A late ammonite that grew shells a metre across, among the last of its kind, in the seas of the final Cretaceous stages worldwide.

Panderodus.note: A long-lived conodont whose cone-shaped elements are in almost every Ordovician and Silurian limestone; the animal itself was a small eel-like swimmer.

Pentremites.note: A blastoid: a bud-shaped echinoderm on a stalk, with five feeding grooves, so abundant in the Mississippian of the Mississippi valley that they are sold by the jar.

Perisphinctes.note: A large evolute ammonite with forked ribs, common enough in the Oxfordian to be found in Europe, East Africa, Cuba and Japan.

Phacops.note: The trilobite with the compound eyes of stacked calcite lenses, each one visible to the naked eye; a Devonian reef-dweller found enrolled by the hundred.

Pikaia.note: A lancelet-like swimmer from the Burgess Shale with a notochord and V-shaped muscles: one of the oldest chordates.

Platecarpus.note: A mid-sized mosasaur, the commonest in the Kansas chalk, preserved with skin, a forked tail fin and the contents of its gut.

Platycrinites.note: A crinoid with a twisted stem and a low cup, from the Mississippian crinoid gardens of Indiana and Iowa where sea lilies grew in meadows.

Platystrophia.note: A strongly ribbed brachiopod with a sharp fold, so common in Cincinnatian rocks that it is Ohio's state fossil in all but name.

Pleurotomaria.note: A slit-shelled sea snail of Jurassic and Cretaceous shelves; its relatives survive today only in deep water.

Protostega.note: A three-metre sea turtle of the Western Interior Seaway, ancestor in form to Archelon, with a shell reduced to struts.
Protostega.conf_note: European 'Protostega' are old referrals; the genus is the Niobrara

Ptychagnostus.note: A tiny blind agnostid trilobite that drifted worldwide, which is what makes it the middle Cambrian's best time-marker.

Ptychodus.note: A shark with pavement teeth for crushing clams, ten metres long, a Cretaceous durophage whose teeth litter the chalk seas of two hemispheres.

Rafinesquina.note: A wide, flat strophomenid brachiopod that lay on the mud like a dropped coin, the most abundant shell in the Ordovician limestones of the American Midwest.

Rhaetavicula.note: The 'Rhaetic bone bed' bivalve, small and asymmetric, crowding the last sea floors of the Triassic in Europe.

Rhomaleosaurus.note: A seven-metre pliosaur of the Early Jurassic, with nostrils built to smell under water, from the same Yorkshire and Somerset shales as Dactylioceras.

Sacabambaspis.note: A jawless armoured fish of Ordovician Gondwana, tadpole-shaped with a bony head shield, in shoals along the Bolivian shore.

Saurichthys.note: A pike-shaped ray-finned fish with a long toothed snout, an ambush predator of Triassic seas and lakes worldwide.

Squalicorax.note: The crow shark, a scavenger of the Cretaceous seas whose serrated teeth are found lodged in dinosaur bones washed out to sea.

Stethacanthus.note: A shark whose males carried an anvil-shaped fin on the back topped with a brush of tooth-like scales: display, most likely.

Streptelasma.note: A solitary horn coral, the simplest of the rugose corals, standing on its tip in the Ordovician mud.

Tentaculites.note: Ringed, tapering shells a centimetre long, in such numbers that they pave Devonian bedding planes; what the animal was is still argued.

Thalassinoides.note: Thalassinoides: the branching burrow systems of shrimps and their forebears, a trace fossil that turns Cretaceous chalk and Jurassic limestone into a network of tunnels.

Thalattosauria.note: Thalattosaurs, long-tailed marine reptiles of the Triassic with pointed down-turned snouts, from the shores of Panthalassa and the Tethys.

Timorites.note: A Late Permian ammonoid with complex sutures on the road to the ammonites proper, from the Tethyan reefs of Timor.

Titanichthys.note: A placoderm as long as Dunkleosteus but with no teeth: a filter-feeder, the first giant to make a living straining the sea.

pbdb.homonym: the PBDB's match is a Cretaceous-Eocene form, not the Devonian placoderm

Toxochelys.note: A metre-long sea turtle of the Niobrara chalk, close to the stem of the living sea turtles.

Trachyceras.note: A knobbly ceratitid ammonoid of the Carnian, in the Alps and the Tethys; its extinction near the Carnian Pluvial Episode.

Trigonia.note: A thick, ornamented triangular clam that burrowed Jurassic and Cretaceous sands worldwide; a lone survivor, Neotrigonia, still lives off Australia.

Tropites.note: A globular Carnian ammonoid, the zone fossil of the late Carnian on both sides of Pangaea.

Uintacrinus.note: A stalkless crinoid that drifted in colonies of hundreds and sank together, leaving slabs of the Kansas chalk covered in its arms.

Waagenoconcha.note: A spiny productid brachiopod that anchored itself in soft mud with hair-fine spines, a Permian shell of cool and warm seas alike.

Xenacanthus.note: A freshwater shark with an eel's body and a long spine at the back of the head, hunting the coal-swamp rivers and lakes for a hundred million years.
